Gramme's 1873 dynamo supplied the reliable current that let Edison run his carbon-filament bulb continuously in homes and streets.
Edison's 1883 observation of current crossing a bulb's vacuum led Fleming to patent the thermionic valve, the diode, in 1904.
Luther's 1517 Ninety-Five Theses and his later German writings founded the Lutheran movement and its distinct doctrinal identity.
Printing presses multiplied Luther's pamphlets and vernacular Bible translations, spreading Lutheran ideas across German lands within years.
Renaissance humanist philology, notably Erasmus's 1516 Greek New Testament, gave Luther the textual tools to challenge Church doctrine.
Postmodern thinkers reacted against modernism's faith in universal reason and progress, rejecting its grand narratives and aesthetic purity.
Postwar disillusionment after the atrocities of total war eroded confidence in progress and totalizing ideologies, fostering postmodern skepticism.
The 1569 Union of Lublin fused the Polish Crown and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania into one commonwealth with a shared Sejm and king.
Lithuania's strain against Muscovite invasion in the Livonian War pushed it to accept full union with Poland at Lublin in 1569.
Napoleon's 1804 proclamation of the French Empire led Francis II to proclaim the Austrian Empire the same year to preserve Habsburg imperial parity.
Defeats in the Napoleonic Wars, including Austerlitz in 1805, ended the Holy Roman Empire in 1806 and forced Habsburg reorganisation into a new empire.
Gunpowder charges packed into iron or ceramic casings produced the explosive bombs of the thirteenth century, such as Song-dynasty thunder-crash devices.
Faraday's 1831 discovery that changing magnetic fields induce current showed how coils oppose changes in current, defining inductance.
Sturgeon's 1825 electromagnet demonstrated the coil-and-core arrangement on which practical inductors depend.
Frederick II's Sicilian court poets in the Kingdom of Sicily developed the sonnet form in the 1230s and 1240s.
Alfred Nobel patented dynamite in 1867 by absorbing nitroglycerine into diatomaceous earth, making a stable and transportable explosive.
Kublai Khan proclaimed the Yuan dynasty in 1271 and went on to complete the conquest of Song China in 1279.
Mongol conquests under Genghis Khan and his successors created the empire whose Chinese branch Kublai Khan turned into the Yuan.
Mongol armies under Kublai Khan conquered the Southern Song between 1276 and 1279, completing the territory the Yuan ruled.
Mongol armies destroyed the Jin dynasty of northern China in 1234, giving the Mongols the North China base that became the Yuan core.
The Yuan's collapse amid mass rebellion let Zhu Yuanzhang drive the Mongols out in 1368 and found the Ming dynasty.
After the Yuan fell in 1368, its remnant Mongol court retreated north and persisted as the Northern Yuan until 1691.
Fear that Nazi Germany was building a bomb prompted Einstein's 1939 letter and the US Manhattan Project that produced the 1945 weapons.
Heavy US casualties on Okinawa in 1945 made invasion estimates grim, strengthening planners' case for using the atomic bombs.
The 1978 Saur Revolution brought the communist PDPA to power, and the Soviet Union intervened in December 1979 to prop up its government.
Arab volunteers recruited to fight the Soviets in Afghanistan, including Osama bin Laden, founded al-Qaeda in 1988.
Soviet withdrawal in 1989 ended Moscow's support for Najibullah's regime, and the mujahideen fought for control of Afghanistan in the civil war.
After the Soviet withdrawal and the collapse of Najibullah's government in 1992, mujahideen parties formed the Islamic State of Afghanistan.
Qin conquered its rivals one by one during the Warring States period, ending centuries of interstate war and creating the first unified Chinese state in 221 BC.
Qin Shi Huang, king of Qin, completed the conquest of the six rival states in 221 BC and proclaimed himself the first emperor.
Qin's decisive victory over Zhao at Changping in 260 BC opened the path to conquest of the rival states.
After Qin collapsed, the Qin general Zhao Tuo seized Guangdong and Vietnam and proclaimed the Nanyue kingdom around 204 BC.
Sturgeon's 1825 electromagnet established the coil-and-core force on which early electric motors, such as Jacobi's 1834 machine, depended.
Faraday's 1821 electromagnetic rotation device showed that electric current produces continuous mechanical motion.
Charles I's failed Bishops' Wars against the Scots left him bankrupt and forced him to summon Parliament, which turned against him and precipitated war.
After the king's defeat and execution in 1649, Parliament's victorious New Model Army ruled through the Rump and proclaimed a republic called the Commonwealth.
The collapse of the republic after Cromwell's death and the army's disarray led Parliament to invite Charles II back, restoring the monarchy in 1660.
The 1641 Irish rebellion and reports of royal complicity made Parliament distrust the king's control of the army, pushing both sides toward war.
Disputes over the Church of England's liturgy and governance between Anglican bishops and Puritan reformers deepened the religious division behind the war.
Napoleon III's dispute with Russia over Holy Places in Jerusalem and his push for prestige led France to join Britain against Russia in 1854.
Nicholas I's push for Russian influence over Ottoman Orthodox subjects and the Danubian principalities triggered the Russo-Ottoman war that drew in Britain and France.
Nazi Germany's ideology and expansionism drove the 1936 Rome-Berlin Axis and 1940 Tripartite Pact that formed the Axis powers.
The Great Depression's economic collapse strengthened fascist and militarist movements in Germany, Italy and Japan, the states that formed the Axis.
Ottoman control of eastern Mediterranean and overland trade routes after 1453 pushed Portuguese and Spanish crowns to seek direct sea routes to Asia.
Renaissance curiosity and advances in cartography and nautical science encouraged systematic overseas exploration by Portugal and Spain.
Dada artists rejected modernist notions of art and rational progress, staging anti-art provocations in Zurich from 1916 that mocked bourgeois culture.
Expressionist painters and poets in Germany pursued emotional distortion and anti-bourgeois revolt, aesthetics that Dada radicalised.
Dada's Paris circle, led by André Breton, turned Dada's provocations toward dream and the unconscious, founding Surrealism in 1924.
Duchamp's readymades and Dada's challenge to art institutions anticipated the postwar critique of originality and high-art boundaries.
Parthian nomads under Arsaces seized Parthia from Seleucid control around 247 BC, founding the independent Arsacid Parthian state.
Greco-Bactria's secession from the Seleucids weakened Seleucid control of the eastern satrapies, enabling Parthian expansion.
Bell Labs' point-contact transistor of 1947 provided the solid-state switching element that Kilby and Noyce combined into the first integrated circuits.
Computer makers' demand for smaller, faster logic and military computing contracts drove Fairchild and Texas Instruments to commercialise integrated circuits.
Integrated-circuit technology let Intel fit a complete central processing unit onto one chip, producing the 4004 microprocessor in 1971.
The French Revolutionary government adopted the guillotine in 1792 as the standard method of execution under its new penal laws.
Enlightenment penal reformers argued for equal, humane execution, and Guillotin's 1789 proposal reflected that egalitarian rationale.
Muslim armies inspired by the Islamic expansion crossed into Iberia in 711 and conquered the Visigothic kingdom.
The Umayyad Caliphate sent Tariq ibn Ziyad's expeditionary army across the strait in 711, launching the conquest that created Al-Andalus.
The early Muslim conquests across the Middle East and North Africa built the military and administrative base from which Iberia was invaded.
Berber troops from Ifriqiya formed the bulk of the 711 invasion force that conquered the Visigothic kingdom.
Christian kingdoms in northern Iberia launched a centuries-long campaign to retake territory from Al-Andalus, the Reconquista.
Christian resistance in the northern mountains under Pelagius created the Kingdom of Asturias as a base against Muslim rule.
Scholars in Córdoba and Toledo translated Greek and Arabic science and philosophy, making Al-Andalus a major centre of the Islamic Golden Age.
Frederick II's 1740 seizure of Silesia from Austria left Maria Theresa determined to recover it, prompting her 1756 alliance with France.
Anglo-French rivalry over North American and Indian trade, escalating in the Ohio Valley, made colonial clashes the war's central conflict.
The enormous debt France incurred fighting the Seven Years' War forced Louis XVI to seek new taxes, precipitating the fiscal crisis behind 1789.
Gothic architecture and sculpture evolved directly out of Romanesque forms, with pointed arches and ribbed vaults replacing rounded ones in 12th-century France.
Capetian royal patronage in the Île-de-France, centred on Abbot Suger's rebuilding of Saint-Denis from 1140, launched the Gothic style.
Theodosius I's death in 395 left the empire permanently divided between his sons, giving the Western half its own emperor, Honorius.
Decades of civil war, plague and invasion in the third century drained Rome's finances and army, weakening the western state for generations.
The Gothic victory at Adrianople in 378 killed Emperor Valens and let Goths settle inside the empire as armed federates.
Germanic peoples, pushed by Hunnic pressure, crossed the frontiers and carved out kingdoms such as those of the Visigoths and Vandals inside Roman territory.
Constantine's founding of Constantinople in 330 shifted imperial resources and attention eastward, leaving the western provinces with weaker defences.
After Rome's western rule collapsed, Visigothic kings consolidated their settlement in Gaul and Iberia into a kingdom that lasted until 718.
Vandal conquest of Roman North Africa in the 430s, exploiting the western empire's weakness, created an independent Vandal kingdom.
Theodoric the Great, King of the Ostrogoths, ruled Italy from 493 after the western emperor was deposed, founding an independent Ostrogothic kingdom.
Clovis and the Franks extended their rule over Gallo-Roman territory in the vacuum left by the western empire, founding the Frankish realm.
Tatar princes under the Golden Horde's collapse in the 1430s split off to found the Khanate of Kazan, which kept Horde-derived rule on the Volga.
Golden Horde authority fragmenting in the 1460s let Astrakhan's Chinggisid prince establish a successor khanate on the lower Volga.
Nogai clans of the former Golden Horde separated into an autonomous Nogai Horde that dominated the northern Caspian steppe.
Moscow's princes collected tribute for the Golden Horde and used that role to extend their territory, laying the basis of the Grand Principality.
Cold War containment led the United States to back Ngo Dinh Diem's Saigon government after 1954 as a non-communist bulwark in Vietnam.
The 1957 Treaty of Rome created the European Economic Community and its Commission as the executive body.
Postwar determination to prevent another European war between France and Germany drove the six founders to pool economic institutions.
The Commission's single-market and institutional role was carried into the European Union that the 1992 Maastricht Treaty created.
The 1868 Meiji Restoration overthrew the Tokugawa shogunate and established a centralised imperial state that became the Empire of Japan.
Commodore Perry's 1854 Convention of Kanagawa forced Japan to open ports, convincing samurai reformers that Western-style modernisation was necessary.
Britain's victory over Qing China in the First Opium War alarmed Japanese elites and accelerated calls for military and institutional reform.
Japanese forces entered Korea in 1894 and attacked Qing China, launching the First Sino-Japanese War that Japan won decisively.
Japan's 1937 advance from the Marco Polo Bridge incident launched full-scale invasion of China, starting the Second Sino-Japanese War.
The Kwantung Army of the Empire of Japan seized Manchuria in 1931 and in 1932 established the puppet state of Manchukuo under Puyi.
Japan's refusal to surrender after the 1944-45 Pacific campaigns led the United States to drop atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945.
Bolshevik Red Army victories in the Russian Civil War overthrew the independent Azerbaijan Democratic Republic in 1920, creating the Azerbaijan Soviet Socialist Republic.
The collapse of the Russian Empire during World War I opened the Caucasus to independence movements and then to Bolshevik conquest.
Soviet-era decision to place Nagorno-Karabakh inside Azerbaijan SSR left an Armenian-majority region under Baku, underlying the 1991 Artsakh secession.
Lincoln's 1860 election on an antislavery platform triggered secession by Deep South states, which formed the Confederacy in February 1861.
The Confederate states' secession and their April 1861 attack on Fort Sumter began the American Civil War.
Electric motors powering suction fans made the 1901 electric vacuum cleaner of Hubert Booth practical for domestic use.
The Nazi regime built the Gestapo in 1933 from Prussia's political police under Göring, and Himmler later extended it nationwide.
Gestapo officers, including the RSHA's Jewish affairs section under Eichmann, organised the deportations of Jews to extermination camps.
The collapse of central authority across the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period created the conditions Zhao Kuangyin exploited to reunify China under the Song.
General Zhao Kuangyin seized the throne from the last Later Zhou emperor in 960 and proclaimed the Song dynasty.
Song military engineers developed gunpowder bombs and incendiary devices, the explosive weapons that appear in 1221 bomb records.
Alexander's withdrawal from the Punjab in 325 BC left satrapies vacant and Greek garrisons that Chandragupta Maurya subsequently overthrew.
Magadha, the most powerful of the Mahajanapadas, supplied the territorial and military base from which the Mauryan state expanded.
Pushyamitra Shunga, a Mauryan general, killed the last Maurya ruler around 185 BC and seized the throne, founding the Shunga Empire.
After Mauryan authority collapsed in the Deccan, Satavahana rulers consolidated independent power there, founding the Satavahana dynasty.
Chandragupta Maurya's victory over Seleucus I around 305 BC forced the Seleucid ruler to cede territory west of the Indus.
Franco-Piedmontese victories over Austria in 1859 gave Piedmont Lombardy, and the Sardinian kingdom then expanded into the Italian peninsula as the Kingdom of Italy.
Napoleon III's secret 1858 Plombières agreement with Cavour committed French troops to the war against Austria that enlarged the Piedmontese state.
Italian nationalism of the Risorgimento, promoted by Mazzini and Garibaldi's supporters, gave the unification movement its popular mass base.
Piedmont-Sardinia's participation in the Crimean War earned Cavour a seat at the 1856 Paris Congress and diplomatic support for Italian unification.
The election of Rudolf of Habsburg as German king in 1273 launched the dynasty's rise to dominance within the Holy Roman Empire.
After the Hungarian defeat at Mohács in 1526, Habsburg claims through the Jagiellon succession gave the dynasty the Hungarian and Bohemian crowns.
Napoleon's return from Elba in March 1815 prompted the Allies to reassemble, and his decision to attack Wellington and Blücher caused the battle at Waterloo.
Wellington and Blücher's victory at Waterloo let the Allies restore Louis XVIII to the French throne, inaugurating the Bourbon Restoration.
Lombard invasions of northern Italy from 568 drove refugees into the Venetian lagoon, where they founded the settlements that became Venice.
Attila's Hunnic raids of the 450s and later Germanic invasions pushed Italian populations onto the lagoon islands for refuge.
Alexander's conquests and his death in 323 BC produced the Diadochi, whose general Seleucus founded the Seleucid state in Asia.
Ptolemy's 312 BC victory at Gaza over Demetrius let Seleucus return to Babylon, the event that began the Seleucid era.
Antiochus IV's suppression of Jewish worship and imposition of Greek cult in Judea provoked the Maccabean revolt of 167 BC.
Antiochus III's war with Rome ended in defeat at Magnesia, and the Roman-imposed Treaty of Apamea in 188 BC stripped Seleucid territory west of the Taurus.
The Bolsheviks' October 1917 seizure of power let them establish Soviet government in Ukraine, which became the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic in 1919.
Bolshevik forces destroyed the Ukrainian People's Republic in 1919 and 1920, clearing the way for a wholly Soviet Ukrainian government.
The Polish-Soviet War of 1919 to 1921 and the Treaty of Riga fixed the western frontier that set the Ukrainian SSR's border with Poland.
The collapse of the Russian Empire during World War I opened the way for Ukrainian independence movements and then Bolshevik conquest.
The 1707 Act of Union created a single Parliament of Great Britain whose leading minister, Walpole, from 1721 developed the office of Prime Minister.
The Hanoverian monarchs George I and George II, with limited English and frequent absences, left cabinet business to ministers, cementing their leadership.
The Reformation's challenge to papal authority supplied the doctrinal and political climate in which Henry VIII broke with Rome and founded the Church of England.
Henry VIII's Act of Supremacy of 1534 made the king head of the English church after the Pope refused his annulment, creating the Church of England.
Charles V's troops sacked Rome in 1527, leaving Pope Clement VII dependent on the emperor and unable to grant Henry VIII's annulment.
Luther's writings gave English reformers such as Tyndale the scriptural arguments against papal authority that shaped the English break with Rome.
WWII weakened the European colonial powers and inspired independence movements in Asia and Africa, whose leaders gathered at Bandung in 1955 to seek a non-bloc path.
Torricelli's 1643 mercury tube experiment demonstrated atmospheric pressure, producing the first barometer.
Galileo's observation that pumps raised water only about ten metres prompted the vacuum experiments that led Torricelli to the barometer.
